paragraphs.text: Ordinarily, there is no riskier step that a scientist can take than to make generalizations from in the universe, but compelling arguments to suggest that there is life on other planets. The reasoning is easy: if our solar system is not unusual, then there are almost certainly billions of planets in the universe, of which some will be habitable. To declare that Earth must be the only planet in the universe with life would be a major error.

It is safer to be guided by the notion that we are not special, which is generally known as the Copernican principle, named after the sixteenth-century Polish astronomer Nicholas Copernicus, who established that the Sun was at the center of our solar system. While there is no guarantee that the Copernican principle will guide us correctly for all future scientific discoveries, it has helped us realize that not only is Earth not the center of the solar system, but the solar system is not in the center of our galaxy, and that our galaxy is not in the center of the universe.

If so, then how can the appearance, or the chemistry, of life on Earth provide clues to what life might be like elsewhere in the universe? Aliens need not look like us to resemble us in more fundamental ways. The three most abundant and chemically active elements in the universe are hydrogen, carbon, and oxygen. These are also the principal three ingredients in life on Earth, with these elements accounting for over 95% of the atoms in the human body and all known life. The chemical structure of carbon allows it to bond readily and strongly with itself and with many other elements in multiple ways, which is why we are considered to be carbon-based life. For this reason, we can be confident that life elsewhere will be composed of a similar mix of elements.

On Earth algae, beetles, jellyfish, snakes, condors, and giant sequoias all co-exist. If you didn't know better, you would be hard-pressed to believe that they all came from the same universe, much less the same planet. Given the diversity of life on Earth, it can be assumed that life elsewhere in the universe, intelligent or otherwise, will look at least as exotic as some of Earth's own life forms.

Let us assume, for the sake of argument, that humans are the only species in the history of life on Earth to evolve high-level intelligence. If life on Earth offers any measure of life elsewhere in the universe, then intelligence must be rare. By some estimates, there have been more than ten billion species in the history of life on Earth. It follows that among all extra-terrestrial life forms we might expect no better than about one in ten billion to be as intelligent as we are, and even if these life forms existed, they may have neither advanced technology nor a desire to communicate across the vast distances of interstellar space.

Should such a civilization exist, radio waves would be the communication band of choice because of their ability to traverse the galaxy unimpeded by interstellar gas and dust clouds But we have understood the electromagnetic spectrum for less than a century. For most of human history, had aliens tried to send radio signals we would have been incapable of receiving them. Aliens may have already done this and concluded that there was no intelligent life on Earth. A more humbling possibility would be that aliens became aware of the technologically proficient species that now inhabits Earth, yet drew the same conclusion.

Based on life on Earth, we naturally take the existence of liquid water to be a prerequisite for life elsewhere. A planet's orbit should not be too close to its star, otherwise the planet's water content would vaporize. The orbit should not be too far away either, or else water would freeze. It is also believed that the evolution of life will involve a planet in a stable, nearly circular orbit around a single star. With binary and multiple star systems, which comprise TS about half of all stars in the galaxy, planetary orbits tend to be elongated, which induces extreme temperature swings that would undermine the evolution of life. Sufficient time for evolution to run its course is essential. Particularly massive stars are so short-lived that life on an Earth-like planet in orbit around them would never have a chance to evolve.

Astronomers often work with what is known as the Drake equation, which is best seen as an interesting idea rather than an objective statement of how the physical universe works. It is a method of calculating how likely it is that a particular set of conditions exist elsewhere in the universe that could have led to the development of an advanced civilization. Doing the calculations provides scientists with an estimate for the total number of intelligent, technologically proficient civilizations in the galaxy. Different scientists have come up with wildly different estimates ranging from one to millions, depending on their individual judgment and areas of expertise.

The discovery of extra-terrestrial intelligence would lead to a change in human self-perception that may be impossible to anticipate. My only hope is that every other civilization isn't doing exactly what we are doing, because then everybody would be listening for signals but nobody would be transmitting them, and it might therefore be concluded that there is no other intelligent life in the universe.
